en: An Excerpt from the *Fo shuo pai jing* (The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Pai), translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in the Wu Kingdom.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. There was a great son named Jeta who possessed a garden.
There were eighty *qíng* of fields not far from the city.
The ground was level and even, abounding in various fruit trees, and there were flowing springs and bathing pools everywhere.
These pools were pure and clear, free from crawling insects, bees, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas.
The householder Sudatta personally served the Buddha and received and upheld the five precepts:
not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking intoxicants.
Having realized the Truths, he was a stream-enterer who constantly delighted in practicing charity and relieving the poor; thus people called him Anāthapiṇḍada, "He Who Provides for the Destitute.

When Sudatta wished to build a vihāra for the Buddha, he traveled everywhere examining the ground until he found that only the Jeta Grove was suitable, whereupon he requested to purchase it from Prince Jeta.
Prince Jeta said,
"If you can cover the ground with gold so that there is no empty space between the pieces, then I shall give it to you.
Sudatta replied:
"Very well!
You may purchase it according to whatever price you wish. Jeta said:
"It was merely a jest," he said.
As the litigation raged on, an elder of the state remonstrated, saying,
"Since the price has already been agreed upon and the matter settled, it is not fitting to regret it now."
He then consented to give it to him.
Sudatta thought silently to himself:
"Which treasury will have enough gold?"
Ji thought he was regretting it, saying,
"You stopped because you disliked the high price.
He replied:
"It is not that I am being stingy;
I am merely considering from which treasury I shall draw the gold.
Immediately, he sent men and elephants to carry out the gold, which was gathered and spread across the ground until, in a short while, forty *qǐng* were completely covered.
He was deeply moved and thought:
"The Buddha must surely possess the Great Way, for he has caused this man to regard his treasures with such lightness.
Let the instruction stop here; do not offer any more gold. The park grounds belong to you, but I myself wish to offer the trees to the Buddha."
Because the site was suitable for construction, a vihāra was established there.
Once it was completed, they each invited the Buddha to reside there.
The Buddha stayed together with one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas within it; therefore, it is called the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma.
The king was named Bimbisāra; the entire palace and the people all served the Buddha together, providing the śramaṇas with robes, food, bedding, and medicines as required for their illnesses.
When there is no Buddha in the world, various paths all flourish, just as torches and candles provide light in the darkness of night;
when a Buddha appears in the world, all heterodoxies cease, like fire that no longer emits light once the sun has risen.
Originally, those within the kingdom had collectively served five hundred practitioners of heterodox paths; at this time, all those heterodox and deviant groups were brought to an end.
Thereupon, the various practitioners of heterodox paths became envious and conspired to destroy the Buddha, hoping thereby to receive honor and service.
Her female disciple, named Sundarī, said:
"Master, do not grieve.
I can cause people to no longer revere the Buddha, so that they will serve you as they did before."
"From this day forward, I wish to adorn myself daily and go back and forth between the Buddha and the various śramaṇas.
After one month has passed, you may kill me in secret and bury me among the Jeta Grove trees, while pretending to go out searching for me."
The people will say, "We have often seen this woman coming and going to the monastery.
They will immediately go to the king and report it, requesting that an official search for her; then, weeping, they will bring forth the corpse.
"He speaks of their lustful disorder and lack of intent toward virtuous conduct.
When the people of the country hear this, they will surely abandon the Buddha and come to serve these teachers.
The teachers said:
"Very well.
The woman followed his instructions and came and went for one month.
The master then ordered four men to kill her together and bury her.
Having searched everywhere, they went to the palace gate and reported:
"A daughter has been lost; everyone saw her going to and coming from the various śramaṇas day after day. We, the officials, have been searching for her."
The King immediately ordered his external officials to escort them.
The masters then feigned wandering back and forth, passing by several times, until they emerged with a bier carrying a corpse. They traveled everywhere wailing and crying out:
"The dharma of the śramaṇas requires that their precepts be pure; yet you have instead committed adultery with another man's wife!"
"Fearing that the matter might be discovered, he killed him and hid [the body]; what kind of Way is this!
When the people of the country heard this, many believed it, for only those who have attained the Way recognize such flattery and hypocrisy.
The Buddha then commanded the śramaṇas:
"Do not enter the city for now.
After seven days, the matter shall be revealed."
On the morning of the eighth day, the Buddha sent Ānanda through the streets to proclaim:

"Those who speak falsehoods and slander others are ordained by Heaven to have foul breath; those who falsely accuse the pure and innocent fall into hell after death; being foolish and cruel, they harbor self-pity and undergo suffering throughout the long night."
When the people of the country heard these words, they all said to one another, "The śramaṇa must be pure, for that is why the Buddha spoke these words.
The king sent men to observe them in secret; they saw members of a heterodox sect secretly congratulating one another and together bestowing gifts upon four people.
According to the methods of the heterodox practitioners, those who know many scriptures receive a large share.
One man was dull-witted and ignorant, and his share was particularly small;
he said in anger, "I shall overturn your affairs!"
Having conspired together to kill someone and falsely accused the Buddha, they instead gave me only a small portion.
A bystander caught them and led them forward to report the matter to the authorities.
Upon arrival, they confessed the truth, and the authorities immediately arrested the conspirators.
The King, together with his ministers, went forth to visit the Buddha;
Anāthapiṇḍada, the lay devotees, and countless citizens of the kingdom all likewise proceeded to visit the Buddha.
Having arrived, they performed their prostrations and sat down to one side.
The king, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Upon hearing this slander, there was no one who did not feel bewildered."
"Only the Buddha is the Truly Enlightened One, pure and immeasurable.
We do not know the reason for this; by what cause does this exist?
The Buddha told the king:
"The arising of slander stems entirely from greed and envy; this has existed for a long time and is not something that began only now.
The King said, "I wish to hear about it."
The Buddha said:

"In my past lives, throughout countless eons, when I was practicing the path of a bodhisattva, I constantly cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, desiring to deliver and liberate all sentient beings."
At that time, there was the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, vast, magnificent, and beautiful, with a flourishing population.
Within it lived a brahmin of the Gautama clan, whose talent and wisdom were profound and far-reaching, making him the foremost in the land.
He had three sons, the youngest of whom was peerlessly handsome.
His father marveled at him greatly and organized a grand assembly, inviting various practitioners and his relatives both near and far, to present the boy to them.
The assembly of masters examined his features and said, "This child loves the Way and possesses the marks of a sage; he will surely become a National Teacher.
Consequently, he was named Pai (Bo).

From his youth, Bo was fond of learning; his talents and arts surpassed those of others, and he was thoroughly versed in all the scriptures as well as the ninety-six kinds of worldly arts and techniques.

He knew nothing he could not understand regarding the destinies of birth and death, mountain collapses and earthquakes, portents, anomalies, blessings and calamities, medical prescriptions, and exorcistic charms;
he was able to repel lustful desires and suppress the arts of sorcery.
He was fully endowed with military strategy and possessed a compassionate and benevolent nature.
After Gautama passed away, his two elder brothers became jealous of him and repeatedly sought a division of the inheritance, saying:
"Pai was fond of learning from his youth and spent much on his teachers; therefore, his share should be small."
The mother took pity on them and repeatedly tried to persuade her two sons, but the two sons would not stop.
Seeing that his elder brother’s resolve was firm, Pai thought to himself:
"All human beings suffer because of their greed."
"If I do not leave, my elder brother will never cease his efforts.
He then informed his mother of his intention to go forth and study the Way; his mother immediately granted him permission.
Pāyāsi departed at once, approached a wise teacher, and became a śramaṇa.
In the mountains, he spontaneously attained the four foundations of mindfulness:
first, to treat all sentient beings with loving-kindness, as a mother loves her child;
second, to feel compassion for the world, desiring to bring about its liberation.
Third, understanding the intent of the Way, their minds are constantly joyful;
fourth, being able to protect themselves, they do not transgress anything.
Furthermore, they attain four further intentions praised by all Buddhas:
First, to restrain lustful desire;
second, to eliminate anger and resentment;
third, to remove deluded thoughts.
Fourth, one does not rejoice in obtaining pleasure nor grieve when encountering suffering.
Furthermore, one severs the five desires:
the eyes do not crave forms;
The ears do not crave sounds;
the nose does not crave fragrances;
the tongue does not crave flavors.
His body does not crave fine or smooth textures.

By means of the path of wisdom and skillful means, he transforms the world in accordance with the truth, causing all to practice the ten wholesome deeds, to be filial and obedient toward their parents, and to serve their teachers and elders with reverence.

To those who harbor doubts, he causes them to believe in the Way and its Virtue, knowing that there is birth after death, that performing good brings forth blessings, that committing evil incurs calamity, and that practicing the Way leads to the attainment of the Way.
Seeing those in distress, he sought to deliver them;
to those who were ill, he provided medicine.
Those who followed the teachings of Puṣya all attained rebirth in heaven after death.
In any commandery or kingdom where floods, droughts, or other calamities occurred, as soon as the planet Puṣya arrived, they were pacified and all toxic harms were eliminated.
At that time, there was a great kingdom, peaceful, blissful, and abundant in people.
The king was named Lambada; the four ministers he appointed were exclusively devoted to wicked flattery, lewdness, theft, villainy, and deception, plundering others without satiety.
The people suffered under their poison, yet the king remained unaware of it.
The Parable (Pai) took pity on him and went outside the city, where he stayed for seven days with a monk named Śāṭa. Only then did he enter the city to beg for food.

From atop his palace, the King saw that the Parable was young, with a dignified and upright appearance and a gait that was extraordinary; feeling great affection and respect, the King immediately came down to greet him.
The king said, "I hope the Master will deign to stay.
I have a vihāra located near the city; you may reside there, and I shall provide whatever you require."
The Parantapa said, "Yes!
The King spoke with joy:
"I wish to comply with your request; from tomorrow onwards, I shall go every day to eat at the palace.
The Parṣad said, "Excellent!"
The king returned and said to his consort, "Bhadra is no ordinary man; you shall see him tomorrow.
The consort was filled with joy.
Beneath the bed was a dog named Piṅgiya; hearing this, it too rejoiced.
The next morning, the Sage entered the palace, and the King and Queen welcomed him, performing a ritual prostration and offering him a golden couch, a woolen rug, and fine cotton blankets.
When the Parable-wisdom (Bodhisattva) was about to take his seat, a dog came forward and licked his feet.
The King rose of his own accord to provide water for washing and respectfully offered him food.
Afterward, they both departed together and arrived at the outer vihāra.

The Parable spoke to the king regarding the laws and regulations for governing the state; the king was greatly pleased and invited the Parable to remain, ordering him to govern state affairs together with his four ministers.
The four ministers were foolish and timid, unaccustomed to battle arrays, and being aware of their own greed and corruption, they were constantly afraid that the king would hear of it.
One minister said:
"When a person dies, their spirit perishes and they are not born again.
Another minister said:
"Poverty and wealth, suffering and joy—all these are the work of Heaven.
Another minister said:
"Performing good brings no blessing; committing evil incurs no calamity."
One minister prided himself on his knowledge of astrology;
yet all were sycophants and flatterers, and did not practice loyal governance.

"The Sage (Pai) is by nature intelligent, possessed of lofty talent and vigor, benevolent, righteous, and respectful. He is trustworthy, compliant, and sparing of speech; when he speaks, his words are always accompanied by a smile, never harming another's feelings. He is pure and free from desire, temperate in his passions, and has few worldly concerns."
His administration was not burdensome; he foreknew calamities and anomalies, could command spirits and deities, and could raise the dead.

He loved the people as his own children and instructed them in the Way—prohibiting them from engaging in idle chatter, hunting or fishing, shooting birds and beasts, killing, stealing, committing adultery, or practicing deception; and forbidding slander, abuse, flattery, envy, strife, anger, or superstitious doubts—he transformed them all toward goodness.
After he took office, the realm was peaceful and secure; wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, and the five grains ripened in abundance.
All officials followed the Dharma and no longer oppressed the people;
the Parantapa remained in non-action, uniquely honored for his devotion to the Buddha.
The śramaṇa practiced the four paths, reciting and studying them morning and evening.
His nephew was also virtuous and resolute, constantly looking up to the sage Pañcaśikha as his teacher.
Those in the kingdom who were fond of learning mostly attached themselves to him.
The King no longer had any further worries, entrusting everything entirely to Pai.
The four ministers, fearing and loathing him, were unable to act as they pleased; they conceived feelings of jealousy and plotted to eliminate Pai.
They pooled their wealth and treasures, amounting to one hundred million in value, and waited for the King to go out. They presented this to the Queen and addressed her thus:
"We, your subjects, with our utmost sincerity, offer all that our household possesses, as well as ourselves, our wives, and our children, to serve as your slaves.
We wish to submit one matter; we pray that you will deign to grant us an audience and consider it."
The queen, greedy for gain, accepted the fine jewels and replied to the four ministers,
saying, "Speak then.
The four ministers answered:
"The *Bhadra* whom Your Majesty honors wears coarse and shabby clothing; he resembles a beggar.
Seeing that his transgressions are grave, he disregards the king's benevolence; daily he guides the Lady toward wickedness and instructs Your Majesty to distance yourself from the inner chambers."
I humbly consider that you, my lady, being in the prime of youth, ought to establish an heir; I fear that if you miss this opportune time, the lineage of our state will be severed.
I pray that you reflect upon this deeply!
"If we do not remove the *bhadra*, I fear there will be regret later.
The consort said in anger,
"The King trusts this man and does not recognize his wickedness."
"Each of you return for now.
I shall worry about this myself; by tomorrow, I will ensure that the Seer (Bodhisattva) is not seen.
The lady then sent the four ministers out and immediately smeared her face with yellow *kucī* (turmeric), disheveled her hair, and lay down.
After a short while, the king returned, and a female attendant informed him,
"The lady is unhappy.
As the king held her in high esteem, he entered and questioned her repeatedly, yet the lady did not respond.
The king then said in anger:
"Who is there that has committed a crime and deserves execution!
Why do you wish to make me commit such a sin against anyone?"
The lady shed tears and said,
"Your Majesty, you simply did not heed my words.
The King replied:
"Speak freely; it shall not contradict you.
The lady then said:
"This morning, as the King was departing, the Seer came and said to me:"
"Now the King is aged and decrepit, unable to attend to the administration of government.
The officials and citizens within the capital all submit to me; we may plot against him and share this pleasure together."
"Yet now, I have been outmaneuvered by this beggar; that is why I am distressed.

When the king heard these words, he was like a man choking: he could neither swallow nor spit it out. Fearing that if he did not employ him he would regret it, yet fearing disorder if he did employ him, he thought:
"Pai has assisted me for twelve years, always governing with loyalty and integrity, worrying over the state to eliminate calamities; both near and far rely upon him."
"This treasure of the kingdom cannot be governed.
The King said,
"If we govern the Seer now, there will surely be great chaos later."
"For the sake of the myriad people, let us endure it together.
Thereupon, the lady threw herself beneath the bed and cried out at the top of her voice:
"If you do not punish Pa, I shall pierce myself with a dagger or throw myself from the tower; I cannot bear to see this!"
The king spoke again to enlighten him, saying:
"You also know the Dharma.
This is no small matter; let us rise and deliberate upon it together."
The lady returned to her seat.
The king said, "The way of the practitioners cannot be met with blades or staves; they must be dismissed gradually by slightly reducing their provisions."
"Those who come tomorrow need not perform prostrations; they should merely raise their hands in a gesture of greeting.
Provide wooden benches for them to sit upon in the courtyard;
cook coarse rice fit for servants and serve it in earthenware vessels."
"When shame and remorse reach such an extreme, one will naturally depart.
When the king spoke these words, Bimbisāra was displeased.
The next morning, the queen immediately conveyed the king’s instructions and gave detailed orders to the royal kitchen.
When the Parivrājaka entered the palace, Bimbisāra’s dog growled and barked at him from beneath the bed.
Seeing the dog bark and observing the lady holding up her curtain and the preparations being made, the Parivrājaka immediately realized there was a plot afoot.
He thought to himself: "I desire to harm no one, yet people turn against me."
Thus, one should avoid [conflict] by retreating into the deep mountains.
A small resentment can grow into something great; it must not be treated lightly.
Since he employs secret plots, I ought to be cautious.
Generally, when a person’s body is frail, practicing with rectitude makes one strong.
Now I already possess my own alms bowl, water flask, leather sandals, umbrella, and water-strainer; these are sufficient for my use.
After the Parṣada had finished eating, he gathered his belongings and prepared to depart.
The king rose in alarm and said,
"What haste is this!"
Looking back, he said to his wife,
"I have caused me to lose the Sage’s favor.
He then stepped forward, took hold of the Seer, and asked:
"Where do you wish to go?
Bhaiṣajyarāja replied,
"I have governed the kingdom for the King for twelve years, yet I have never seen Bimbisāra growling as he does now."
"There must be a plot, which is why they wish to leave.
The King said,
"Indeed there is."
Now that I have observed the intent of the Seer, my awakening is most profound and clear.
I pray you will exhort and rouse yourself; you must execute the evil man!
There is no need for you to depart.
The Parantapa said:
"The King’s former intentions were profound, but now they have grown thin. Since I am without fault, it is fitting that I depart at this time.
For all prosperity is followed by decline, and all unions end in separation; good and evil are impermanent, and calamity and fortune follow one another."
If one forms friendships that are not firm, one cannot be intimate with them; if one is intimate without moderation, there will surely be leakage and profanation over time.
It is like drawing from a spring: if one digs too deep, the water becomes turbid. Associating with the worthy brings wisdom; practicing with the foolish increases delusion.
Frequent meetings give rise to arrogance, while infrequent contact leads to resentment.
One who associates with virtuous friends should come and go at the proper times; though intimate, they should maintain a sense of reverence, so that their bond grows ever more profound over time.
An unwholesome friend is one who pursues a false pretense that does not correspond to reality, using clever speech and sharp rhetoric to feign conformity while lacking sincerity.
If such a person receives me with courtesy, I should respond with respect;
if they treat me with arrogance, I should immediately distance myself from them.
There are those who are affectionate toward one another yet turn to mutual hatred; when they are in love, they may be approached, but when they hate, they must not be drawn near.
One should honor and associate with the good, and use caution to distance oneself from the evil. To make no distinction between good and evil is not the way to peace.
If a person is without fault, one must not intrude upon them recklessly;
once a person has finished their evil deeds, one must not harbor resentment toward them;
if a person wishes to distance themselves from you, one must not force intimacy.
Once affection has been severed, it cannot be pursued through longing.
When a bird’s branch is broken upon which it slept, it knows it must seek another place to roost; in leaving and following, there is what is appropriate—why must one cling to the status quo?
One cannot climb upon withered branches, nor can one violate a mind that is in turmoil.
When people wish to harm one another, they do not rejoice upon meeting; they call out but do not respond in harmony—by this one may know their shallowness.
When people wish to benefit one another, they rush to each other's aid in times of urgency; they speak with loyal admonition—by this one may know their depth.

He does not draw near the good nor distance himself from the evil; he first shows respect and later becomes arrogant, making no distinction between the worthy and the foolish. Why keep him when there is no need?
When this man first came, he prostrated himself; now he merely holds up his scroll.
"If I do not go, I shall be reviled and driven away.
Previously, a golden throne was provided; now, a wooden bed is set out.
Previously, precious vessels were used; now, earthen bowls are employed."
Originally, rice was served as the staple food; now, coarse, inferior rice is provided.
If I do not leave, the rice will eventually be discarded upon the ground.
When acquaintances meet, the host regards them such that after one night they are like gold, after two nights like silver, and after three nights like copper.
"The proof is manifest before our eyes; why wait for anything else?
The King said, "That the land is prosperous and the people are at peace is due to the power of the Seer (Upatiṣya)."
"If we abandon it now, it will later fall into ruin.
The Parable-teller said:
"There are four ways in which the world falls into ruin of its own accord:"
When a tree is thick with flowers and fruit, one breaks its branches;
when a viper harbors venom, it turns against its own body;
when a minister is not virtuous, his harm extends to the state.
When a person performs unwholesome deeds, they enter hell after death.
This constitutes the fourth form of self-destruction.
As the Sūtra says:
"‘Evil arises from the mind, / And in turn it harms itself, / Just as rust born of iron / Consumes and destroys its own form.
The King said:
"The state has no worthy ministers; it truly must rely upon you, Paṇḍita.
If you wish to entrust us to others, we shall surely face peril.
Paṇḍita said:
"Ordinary people have four ways of endangering themselves:
acting as a guarantor for another's household, serving as a witness for others, acting as a matchmaker for others' wives, and listening to and following perverse words.
These are the four ways of endangering oneself."
The Sūtra says:
"When a fool acts, he brings suffering upon himself; by indulging his desires and letting his mind run wild, he later incurs heavy calamity."
The King said, "I hold my teacher and friend, Pañcika, in constant high regard; you must forgive my shortcomings and do not abandon me.
Pañcika replied:
"There are four kinds of friends whom one must know:
there is the friend who is like a flower, the friend who is like a scale, the friend who is like a mountain, and the friend who is like the earth."
What is meant by being like a flower?
When it is fresh, one plucks it to wear in the hair; when it withers, one discards it.
To associate with those who are wealthy and noble, yet abandon them when they are poor and lowly—this is friendship like a flower.
What is meant by being like a scale?
When an object is heavy, the head of the scale dips; when an object is light, it tilts upward.
To show respect when there is something to give, and to be arrogant when there is nothing to give—this is what is called a "scale-like friend."
What is meant by being like a mountain?
It is like a mountain of gold: when birds and beasts gather there, their fur and feathers are suffused with its radiance;
it honors those who are noble and shares in the joy of the wealthy and happy—this is a "mountain friend."
What is meant by being like the earth?
All the hundred grains, wealth, and treasures depend upon it; it bestows, provides, and protects them with profound kindness that is never thin. This is the friendship of the earth.
The King said, "Now I realize for myself that my resolve and thoughts were shallow; having listened to and acted upon wicked words, I have caused Bhadra to depart.
Bhadra said:
"The wise have four things that should not be relied upon:
a false and deceitful friend, a sycophantic and flattering minister, a seductive and treacherous wife, and an unfilial son.
These are the four things not to be relied upon."
The Sūtra says:
"A wicked friend ruins a person; a sycophantic minister throws the court into disorder; a wanton wife destroys a family;
a wicked son endangers his parents."
The king said, "Our mutual affection is deep; you should remember our old friendship and not abandon me in my solitude.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"There are ten matters by which one knows the depth of affection: not forgetting one another when separated by distance;

feeling joy upon meeting; sharing choice delicacies with one another; enduring offensive words; increasing one's delight upon hearing of good deeds; offering loyal counsel upon seeing evil; being able to do what is difficult to do; not disclosing private matters to others; resolving matters of urgency; and not abandoning one another in times of poverty or low status."
These are the ten ways of being affectionate and kind.
The Sūtra says:
"Transforming evil into goodness, refining through the Dharma, and instructing with loyalty and integrity."
"This is the path of friendship based on righteousness. The King said,
"The wickedness of my four ministers has caused Pai to become resentful and no longer take pleasure in me."
The Parable said:
"There are eight signs by which one knows that another does not rejoice in him:

their countenance changes upon seeing him; they cast sidelong or avaricious glances; they do not respond when spoken to; they call right wrong; they take pleasure in hearing of his decline; they are not pleased to hear of his prosperity; they disparage another's virtues; and they promote another's faults."
These are the eight matters.
The Sūtra says:
"Even one who kills while settling a dispute may still have grounds for exoneration; [but there is no such excuse for one who kills out of anger]."
"Harboring poisonous conspiracies— such a mind is difficult to trust.
The King said,
"It was my own stupidity and lack of discernment between light and darkness that led me to be misled by evil people and thus lose the Sage's favor."
The Parable said: "There are ten matters by which one knows a person to be wise:

distinguishing the worthy from the foolish; recognizing the noble from the lowly; knowing the poor from the wealthy; judging what is difficult or easy; clarifying what should be abolished or established; examining who is fit for office; understanding the customs upon entering a state; knowing where to find refuge in times of distress; possessing broad learning and extensive knowledge; and attaining insight into past lives."
These are the ten matters.
The Sūtra says:
“One distinguishes a friend in times of urgency; one sees valor in battle; one knows wisdom through debate.”
"When grain is expensive, one recognizes benevolence. The King said,
"Since I obtained the Paṇḍita, both those within and without my realm have been peaceful and secure."
"Today you abandon me, and I shall forever have nothing to rely upon.
The Sage said:
"There are eight things by which one may find peace and stability:"

One obtains paternal wealth, possesses wholesome karma, achieves one's studies, has virtuous friends, a chaste and kind wife, filial and compassionate children, obedient servants, and is able to distance oneself from evil.
These are the eight matters.
The Sūtra says:
"To be born with wealth, to find a virtuous friend—how joyful! To refrain from committing any evils,"
"It is a blessing and a joy.
The King said,
"The words of the Sage are indeed nothing but joyful."
The Parable said: "There are eight things that bring joy:

to associate with the virtuous; to have the opportunity to consult with sages; to possess a nature that is harmonious and benevolent; to see one's undertakings renewed daily; to be able to restrain one's anger; to be able to anticipate and prevent calamities; to be mutually affectionate in the way of the Dharma; and for friends not to deceive one another."
These are the eight matters.
The Sūtra says:
“It is a joy that a Buddha has appeared; it is a joy that he expounds the path of the Sūtras; it is a joy that the assembly is harmonious.”
"Harmony brings constant peace.
The King said, "Pai was always easy to advise; why is he so difficult to keep now?"
The Parable said:
"There are ten who should not be admonished:

the stingy and greedy, those who lust after beauty, the dull-witted, the impetuous and violent, the obstinate and aggressive, those who are utterly exhausted, the arrogant and self-indulgent, those who delight in strife, the exclusively foolish, and the base person."
These are the ten.
The Sūtra says:
"To speak the Dharma to one who is exclusively foolish is like conversing with the deaf; such a person is difficult to transform."
"He cannot be exhorted or enlightened. The King said,
"As I am so arrogant and self-indulgent, I am unable to distance myself from sensual pleasures."
“Has the Parable attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that he no longer speaks with me?
The Parable replied:
“There are ten circumstances under which a person does not speak with one:”
Arrogance, dullness, anxiety and fear, delight in anticipation, shame and modesty, stammering, resentment, hunger and cold, worldly affairs, and meditative reflection.
These are the ten matters.
The Sūtra says:
"It is permissible to speak what one can practice; do not speak empty words for what you cannot."
"Deceitful and lacking sincerity, she is one whom the wise do not regard.
The King said,
"This wicked woman has a beautiful appearance and is skillful in speech."
"If there is an external paramour, how can one suddenly come to know of him?
The Seer said,
"There are ten signs by which he may be known at once:"

The hair on his head is disheveled and falls askew; his complexion changes and he breaks into a sweat; he speaks and laughs with a loud voice; his gaze is not upright; he accepts precious ornaments; he stares vacantly at the walls; he sits uneasily in his place; he frequently visits neighbors; he delights in going out for excursions in the wild; and he takes pleasure in consorting with courtesans.
These are the ten matters.
The sutra says:
"Women are difficult to trust; their clever tongues delude people. Therefore, the noble man—"
"To be distant yet not intimate.
The King said, "In human nature,
one is drawn close to and places trust in women, unaware of their wickedness."
The Parable said: "There are ten kinds of persons whom one must not trust:

those favored by their lord; those intimate with women; those who rely on their own physical strength and health; those who depend on their wealth and property; those dwelling in places flooded by great waters; those in dilapidated houses with crumbling walls; those where dragons and serpents reside; those who defraud the government; those of long-standing evil character; and poisonous, harmful insects."
These are the ten.
The Sūtra says:
“It is said that one may drink wine without becoming intoxicated; it is said that one may be intoxicated without losing self-control; and that a ruler may be fond of his wife.”
"None of these can be relied upon with confidence.
The King said, "As Pa said, the cultivation of attachment gives rise to evil; this is indeed to be loathed."
The Parable said:
"There are five things to be loathed:
harsh speech that injures others; slandering and maliciously inciting strife; fretful and unpleasing speech; jealousy and cursing; and double-tonguedness with face-to-face deception."
These are the five.
The Sūtra says:
"To exert oneself in labor for others, yet desire to receive their blessings—calamity shall fall upon one's own person."
"One will encounter widespread enmity oneself.
The King asked,
"What actions must one perform to be loved and respected by others?"
The Parable said: "There are five qualities of love and respect:

being gentle and capable of endurance; being cautious and trustworthy; being diligent and sparing of speech; having one's words and deeds correspond with each other; and becoming more steadfast the longer one associates with another."
These are the five.
The Sūtra says:
“One who knows how to cherish the body / Carefully guards what they maintain / And sets their aspirations on the lofty and far-reaching.”
"The Master of Studies is not deluded.
The King asked,
"Who is it that is despised by others?"
The Parable said: "There are five kinds of arrogance: arrogance regarding long hair;

arrogance regarding impure clothing; arrogance regarding being empty and lacking purposeful thought; arrogance regarding lewd conduct and lack of propriety; and arrogance regarding unrestrained jesting."
These are the five.
The Sūtra says:
"Gathering the mind to follow what is right, like a horse well-tamed and controlled, one is free from the habit of arrogance."
"He is revered by gods and men.
The King said, "I pray that you,
Paṇḍita, will take heed and return with me to the vihāra!"
The Parable said:
"There are ten things that should not be admitted into the hall:

a wicked teacher, a depraved friend, one who treats the sages with contempt, one who opposes the teachings, lewdness, a fondness for wine, a stingy and oppressive elder, an ungrateful son, a woman who lacks self-restraint, and a maidservant or concubine who is overly preoccupied with her own adornment."
These are the ten.
The Sūtra says:
"Keep far away from evil people; do not befriend those who are licentious and dissolute; attend upon the worthy."
"Thus one achieves illustrious virtue.
The King said,
"Pa has brought joy to me, and there is no trouble in the four quarters."
"If you depart today, the people of the kingdom will surely lament.
The Sage said,
"There are eight things by which one may find peace and happiness:"

He served his teachers and elders with propriety and led the people through filial piety; he was humble and modest toward all, harmonious and benevolent by nature, rescuing those in peril and rushing to their aid, exercising empathy and loving others as himself, lightening taxes and frugality in expenditure, and forgiving grievances while remembering old kindnesses.
These are the eight matters.
The sutra says:
"Cultivate the roots of all virtues; act only after careful deliberation; save human life alone."
"You shall enjoy peace and happiness for the rest of your life.
The King said, "I constantly think of Pa; how could I ever forget him?"
The Parable said: "The wise possess twelve reflections: at the crowing of the cock, they reflect on repentance and the cultivation of merit;

rising early, they reflect on prostrating to their kin and honoring the venerable; facing affairs, they reflect on the need for preparedness; regarding their dwelling, they reflect on avoiding harm and danger; in speech, they reflect on being sincere; upon seeing faults, they reflect on admonishing with loyalty; toward the poor, they reflect on providing compassion and protection; possessing wealth, they reflect on practicing generosity; regarding food and drink, they reflect on moderation; in feeding others, they reflect on impartiality; in leading a multitude, they reflect on bestowing kindness; and regarding military equipment, they reflect on timely maintenance."
These are the twelve.
The Sūtra says:
"Cultivate one's duties, provide for them with foresight, and let one's undertakings be renewed daily."
"He will never miss the proper time.
The king asked,
"How can we obtain a great sage to cause the Seer (Bhadraka) to remain?"
The Parable said: "A great sage possesses ten qualities:

his conduct, learning, and reputation are lofty and far-reaching; he does not violate the scriptures or precepts; he reveres the Triple Gem of the Buddha; he receives what is good and never forgets it; he restrains desire, anger, and delusion; he practices the four immeasurable minds; he delights in performing acts of kindness and virtue; he does not disturb sentient beings; he is able to transform those who are unrighteous; and he maintains order such that good and evil do not become confused."
These are the ten practices.
The Sūtra says:
"A person of wisdom is difficult to encounter, yet they do not exist everywhere; wherever they are born,"
"Our kinsmen shall be blessed.
The King said,
"My transgression is grave!"
"By harboring wicked people, you have caused me, the Seer, to depart in anger.
The Seer said:
"There are fifteen great evils: [list follows]"

They delight in killing, plundering, lewdness, fraud, flattery, hypocrisy, sycophancy, calumny, slandering the virtuous, greed and corruption, license, drunkenness, envying the worthy, destroying the Way, and harming the sages, all while disregarding their calamities and sins.
These constitute the fifteenth.
The Sūtra says:
"Deceitful, tyrannical, and gluttonous; resentful and slandering the virtuous; one's own conduct is not upright—"
"Upon death, one will fall into the evil realms.
The King said, "The Parable-master’s admonitions do not cease; they cause me shame."
The Parantapa said: "There are ten things that bring shame:

a ruler who does not understand governance; a minister or son who lacks propriety; one who receives kindness but does not repay it; one who cannot reform their faults; a wife with two husbands; a woman who becomes pregnant before marriage; one whose training has not been perfected; a person who, like one leaning on a weapon, is unable to fight; a miser who watches others practice charity; and a slave who cannot be commanded."
These are the ten.
The Sūtra says:
"If there should be a person in the world who is capable of knowing shame and remorse, they are easy to lead forward."
"It is like driving a fine horse.
The King said, "At first, my thought was this:"
"One who knows the Way is difficult to defeat.
The Parable said:
"There are twelve difficulties:"

It is difficult to employ those who are exclusively foolish; it is difficult to govern those who are timid and weak; it is difficult for those harboring resentment to meet together; it is difficult for those of little learning to engage in debate; it is difficult for the poor to remain free from debt; it is difficult for an army to be without a master general; it is difficult to serve a ruler throughout one's life; it is difficult for one who studies the Way to lack faith; it is difficult for the wicked to hope to be reborn in heaven; it is difficult to be born during the time of a Buddha; it is difficult to hear the Buddha’s Dharma; and it is difficult to receive, practice, and achieve mastery of it—these constitute the twelve difficulties.
The Sūtra says:
“Human life is difficult to obtain; the time of encountering a Buddha is difficult; the Dharma is difficult to hear;
and hearing it and being able to practice it is difficult.”
The King said,
"In conversing with Paṇḍita now, my wisdom has increased.
Paṇḍita replied:
"To state the essentials briefly, there are forty-five matters that people ought to know:
cultivating one's household;
harmonizing one's family;..."
Be affectionate toward one's nine classes of relatives;
be trustworthy toward friends;
and follow an enlightened teacher in one's studies.
The undertaking will surely succeed;
with lofty talent and far-reaching wisdom,
one should maintain oneself through virtue.
When wealthy and noble, practice benevolence;
in managing one's estate, one should be prudent;
when possessing wealth, one ought to expand one's undertakings.
Do not entrust wealth to a child;
associate with those who are virtuous;
do not trust those who merely seek a superficial alliance.
When wealth is held by officials, one should be concerned about its early distribution;
in buying and selling transactions, act with sincerity and do not deceive;
in all places where you lodge, you must first inspect them before staying.
Wherever one goes, one should know the distinction between the noble and the humble;
upon entering a country, one should associate with virtuous people;
as a guest, one should rely upon the powerful.
Do not contend with the powerful;
thus, wealth that has been lost can be sought again.
If you have always been poor, do not harbor great expectations.
Do not show precious objects to others;
do not speak of hidden matters to your wife;
as a ruler, you should honor the worthy.
The generous and brave take up loyalty and trustworthiness;
those who are pure can govern a state;
those who pursue what is right are able to achieve merit.
The principles of edification have filial piety and obedience as their foundation;
the relationship between teacher and disciple values harmony and respect;
if one wishes to have many disciples, one must strive to instruct them according to righteousness.
A physician must possess proven efficacy; if their skill is shallow, they should not be employed.
When one is ill and emaciated, one should follow the physician's instructions;
one should exercise moderation in food and drink.
One should attend to the needs of one's body;
share fine food with others;
and in gambling, do not stake one’s wealth or life.
In matters of giving and lending, one should personally deliver the items with one's own hands;
when acting as a witness, follow the truth and do not wrong the innocent;
admonish the angry with gentleness, and avoid evil through patience.
Among humans, regardless of noble or humble status, harmony of nature is considered good;
in the Way, maintaining the precepts with purity is supreme;
among all the great paths in the world, none surpasses Nirvana.

The Way of Nirvāṇa is free from birth, old age, sickness, and death; hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; it fears neither water nor fire, nor enemies nor thieves; furthermore, it is devoid of affection, craving, and all evils. Since all anxieties and afflictions are extinguished, it is called "extinction" (nirodha).
"May Your Majesty take care of yourself; I now wish to withdraw.
The King said, "If you, Pai, wish to depart, do you have any further parting advice?"
The Parable said:
"For example, where a great flood has swept through and breached the land, even after a hundred years, one ought not to establish a city or fortress there.
The water will surely return, following its old course."
A person of long-standing evil, though they may wish to practice goodness, should not be trusted;
since their fundamental nature has not been extinguished, they may again commit wrongs, and thus one must not fail to exercise caution.
Whatever a person desires to accomplish is like digging a pond: if one digs without ceasing, one will surely find spring water.
All matters develop gradually; the wise perceive the subtle signs and are thus able to preserve their lives.
"It is like a person skilled at swimming who crosses the current.
The King said,
"Everything you have said before and now has pierced my heart."
The men and women of the entire nation were without exception filled with joy;
those who had long harbored ill will were humbled and submissive, none daring to speak out.
I pray that you will hear their words.
"If one were to encounter a strange person, how could one know they are wise?

Bhaṭṭi replied, "One knows a wise person by their responses in dialogue; their various distinctions are such that their speech is never unwholesome, and their teacher’s doctrine is fundamentally correct—it is by this that one knows them."
He understood human nature to be characterized by benevolence, gentleness, prudence, and elegance; by being warm, refined, wise, and broad-minded.
He was an object of admiration for all virtues, of whom no one had any doubt.
Observing his words and deeds, one saw that his heart and mouth were in perfect accord.
Observe their sitting and rising, and whether their movements and stillness are free from frivolity;
examine their conduct in coming and going, as well as their dress and actions—by these one may sufficiently know them.

When conversing with those of great wisdom, one should seek to grasp their underlying intent; yet grasping that intent is difficult, like handling a blade or holding poison—one must not fail to exercise caution.
The King said, "I wish to serve those who are wise so as not to lose their favor; how should I do this?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Revere it without treating it lightly; having heard and received it, you must put it into practice.
The wise recognize the truth and embody the Way of non-action.
Knowing the future, the present, and the past, they realize that all return to emptiness and non-being."
Human beings are like transformations: youth gives way to old age; the strong and healthy fall into decay; those who are born must die; and wealth and status are impermanent.
Therefore, one should remain mindful of danger amidst security, and maintain awareness of impermanence amidst prosperity.
He bestows affection upon the virtuous and casts the unvirtuous far away.
Though he may harbor resentment, he does not inflict harm in return.
He is gentle yet difficult to offend; he is weak yet difficult to overcome.
"One who is as enlightened as this person must not be treated with contempt.
The King said,
"If one serves a man of wisdom with all one's heart, loving and respecting him, will there not surely be merit?"
The Parable said:
"The wise follow the sages and practice benevolence; they delight in enlightening the ignorant and foolish to bring them to human wisdom.
In governing a state, they consider generous bestowal to be good; in cultivating the Way, they consider guiding others to be correct."
When the state faces urgent calamities, one can provide relief; knowing the proper time for advancing or retreating, one harbors no resentment.
Bestowing kindness extensively and practicing great generosity without expecting recompense—one who acts thus shall obtain blessings and remain free from affliction for the rest of their life.
"Your Majesty, do not doubt this: the methods of governing must not lose their way; encouraging the people to learn what is good is the greatest benefit for the state.
The King asked, "Who can detain the *bhadra*?"
"My heart is filled with grief and misery; I am distraught as if mad!
he said, weeping as he turned toward the Seer (Pai), repenting and seeking absolution for his transgressions.
The Seer replied:
"Just as one who cannot swim should not enter deep water, so too one who wishes to take revenge should not provoke others prematurely.
When those who are close and affectionate quarrel, they later apologize to one another; though we know that reconciliation is good, it is not as well as having no quarrel from the beginning."
Goodness cannot be rewarded; instead, you listen to slanderous words.
I am like a flying bird, dwelling in no fixed place.
The Way prizes purity and emptiness; it is not suited for the human world.
Just as a wild fire passes by and scorches the trees in its path;
as turbulent waters wreck a boat, or poisonous insects harm a person—
when engaging with wisdom, one should not cause such disturbance.
Plants and trees differ in their natures; birds and beasts are divided into their respective species;
the white crane is naturally white, and the cormorant is naturally black.
I am distinct from others, having no desire for the world.
It is like an old farmer who has lived his whole life among the mountains and marshes; to give him fine clothes would be of no benefit to him.
In the world there is a tree named Fan-li; the owner planted it himself, yet he could not eat its fruit, while others who stole it were able to enjoy the harvest.
Now, Your Majesty, those who have thus brought peace and stability to the state are driven away,
while the sycophants and deceivers who ruin the administration remain to draw their stipends.
Guests who stay too long weary the host.
"I ought to withdraw.
The King said, "Human life is most precious; I pray you, take this into consideration!"
"Now I wish to rely on my own strength, and my service to the Seer shall surpass that of before.
The Seer said,
"Though the King speaks thus, you still may not receive the gift."
"Madam, my intention is not good, and it is not fitting for me to remain.

Every household in the world has food ready for cooking; the reason a śramaṇa carries an alms bowl to beg is that he personally delights in eliminating greed, maintaining the precepts through non-action, and distancing himself from transgressions."
The king said, "Now that you, Paṇḍita, have departed, do not let our connection be severed forever. I pray that you will come once more at the proper time, so that I may have no cause for regret.
Paṇḍita replied:
"Since we are both capable and strong, we shall still see one another.
For now, I wish to enter the mountains to cultivate my resolve.
Indeed, it is better to be far away and think of each other with kindness than to be near and harbor ill will toward one another."
The wise understand through analogies; please allow me to cite one:

suppose there were a person who smeared a blade with honey. A dog, having found it, licked it and thereby wounded its tongue; yet, because of its craving for the slight sweetness, it remained unaware of the pain of its wound.
"The four ministers are like this: they are eloquent with their mouths alone, yet their hearts are like sharp swords; the King must strictly warn them against this.
From now on, if there is ever cause for alarm or fear, you should constantly call upon Paṇḍaka, and all terrors will surely be dispelled."
The Parable spoke again:
"The owl delights in the cemetery, while the swarm of rats dwells in filth;
the hundred birds nest in trees, yet the crane resides in a foul pond."
All things have their own natures, and their inclinations and desires differ.
I delight in non-action (*wuwei*), just as a king takes pleasure in his kingdom.
Although a vessel may be coarse and worn, it cannot be discarded outright, for each has its own contents to hold.
Even those who are foolish, lowly, and unworthy must not be abandoned, for each has their own use;
Your Majesty should recognize this.
I can still discern the direction of a person's speech and intent, just as when birds gather on a tree, they first alight upon the lower branches and then move upward with a warbling call.
"Seeing Bimbisāra, I knew there was a plot both within and without.
My intention was to weary him of the old so that he might accept the new.
The Paṇḍita said:
"Please withdraw," he said, and immediately rose and departed from the city.
The king and his consort wept as they saw him off; among the people, both young and old, there was none who did not wail in lamentation.
The King went to question Bo and asked,
"Who is trustworthy? Bo replied:

"My nephew is virtuous and wise; he may be consulted. Let us go out together from time to time to tour the kingdom, observing the folk songs and customs of the people so that we may know their conditions."
The King said,
"I shall obey your instructions.
He then prostrated himself before the Seer (Paṇḍita) along with his ministers and the people, and thereupon departed.
"After the Parantapa had departed, the four ministers acted with unrestrained license abroad, governing the state through sycophantic eloquence;
meanwhile, the consort within the palace served the King with seductive charms."
The king’s mind became deluded, and he no longer concerned himself with the affairs of state; indulging in luxury, lust, and pleasure, he remained immersed in debauchery day and night.
The various officials and ministers levied taxes and seized property without any sense of propriety.

In the markets of Zhengping, there were no longer any fixed prices for goods; the strong oppressed the weak, plundering one another in turn, even coming to blows and injury, showing no fear of the laws or prohibitions.
The sons of virtuous citizens were plundered to become slaves; their six kinds of relatives lost one another, fleeing in hiding to eke out a meager existence.
Calamities and anomalies followed one after another, yet the King could not perceive them;
winds and rains were untimely, so that what was sown could not be harvested.
The kingdom was desolate and the people impoverished; hunger filled the roads, and the sounds of lamentation moved even the ghosts and spirits.
The populace was filled with grief and fear, and those who remained were nearly all gone; they traveled on weeping and wailing, none of whom failed to miss the Seer (Bodhisattva).
The Parable was like a hawk soaring above the flocks of birds; he suppressed and subdued the wicked, and nurtured the people and all creatures with compassion, just like Śakra, Lord of the Devas.

Later, the Parable’s sister’s son, who had become a monk, traveled to another district. Seeing that the kingdom was in chaos and turmoil, the villages were destroyed, and the people were destitute and few, he returned and told the King:
"The great ministers do not govern properly; they give free rein to bandits and thieves, plundering and killing the innocent, acting with cruelty and a lack of the Way."
Men resent him and the gods are incensed; Heaven repeatedly sends down calamities.
This is known far and wide, yet the King remains unaware.
If he does not plan for the future without delay, there will soon be no people left.
The king was then startled and said:
"It is indeed as Pai-jie has warned.
Those I have appointed are like wolves among sheep."
"I know that the people are about to disperse like runaway chariots or galloping horses.
Now that you, O Master of the Path, have informed them, how will you instruct them?
The Master of the Path replied:
"The departure of the Parable Master (Pai) and the ensuing chaos in the state are both caused by treacherous ministers.
Your Majesty should devise another plan; the kingdom may yet be restored.
I pray that you will go forth on a tour of inspection once more; with your own eyes and ears, you shall know the truth of the matter."
The king then secretly departed with the practitioner to tour the borders of the kingdom.
There he saw several dozen young women, all between fifty and sixty years of age, their clothes tattered and worn, walking along while sighing and lamenting.
The practitioner asked, "These women are of marriageable age; why have they not married?
They replied:
"I shall cause the royal house to fall into destitution; how joyful I would be!
The practitioner said, "What you say is incorrect."
"The King’s position is exalted; how could he possibly worry about you?
The girl said, "Not so."
The King governs without rectitude, causing the land to suffer famine.
At night we are beset by thieves and bandits; by day we are oppressed by the petty officials.
With food and clothing not provided, who would ever marry me?
The king proceeded further and saw several elderly women whose clothes did not cover their bodies; they were emaciated and blind, walking along while weeping.
The practitioner asked them, "What sorrows do you all have?"
He replied,
"It would be a joy indeed if I could make the king as destitute and blind as I am!
The practitioner said:
"This is not true.
The old man’s own eyes have grown dim; what fault is there on the part of the King?
The mothers said:

"At night I was plundered by thieves, and by day I was seized by officials; I wander in poverty gathering firewood and am afflicted by venomous stings—could this not be the King's own wickedness that has brought me to such a state?"
The king proceeded further and saw a woman kneeling to milk a cow when she was trampled by the animal; falling to the ground, she cursed him, saying:
"May you trample the wife of a king as swiftly as I have been!"
The practitioner asked, "The ox trampled you of its own accord; what fault was there on the part of the royal household?
He replied:

"The King governs without rectitude, causing the state to fall into chaos and disorder; he fails to restrain thieves and bandits, leading to my fine ox being seized and trampled by a vicious one—is this not the fault of the King?"
The practitioner said,
"It is because you yourself lack virtue that you cannot milk the cow.
The woman said:
"It is not so. If the royal house were virtuous, Pāyāsi would have remained of his own accord, and the kingdom would not be in chaos.
The king proceeded further and saw a crow pecking at a frog; the frog cursed it, saying:
"Let it be that the evil king sees himself devoured just as I have been;
how delightful that would be! The practitioner said, "If you are being devoured by crows yourself, will the king protect you?"
He replied:
"I do not hope for protection.

Your Majesty has shown no benevolence, your administration is unjust, and sacrifices have been abandoned; thus, the heavens are parched and the waters are exhausted, which is why my body was seen being devoured by crows."
The frog called out, saying:
"One who understands governance discards a single wicked person to benefit a family; one discards a single wicked family to benefit a village."
"One who does not understand governance causes the people and all things to lose their proper place, leading the world to resentment and litigation. The Daoist said:
"The common people are innocent, yet their sighs and lamentations have moved Heaven; thus the deity has caused the toad to descend and speak these words."
The King has personally witnessed this; he ought to retire the wicked men, reform his past ways, cultivate the future, and begin anew with his people.
If one sows in fertile soil and the rains fall in their proper season, why worry that the harvest will not ripen?
The king asked,
"Who should be appointed now?
The practitioner replied:
"It would be appropriate to urgently invite Bo.
Bo is benevolent, sagacious, and knows the proper timing; if he returns to the kingdom, it will surely be at peace.
Upon returning, the king immediately dispatched a messenger into the mountains to invite Bo, saying:

"If Pa does not return, you should go and prostrate yourself, saying: 'I myself am aware that I have brought grievous offense upon the myriad people; I am so consumed by anxiety that I cannot eat, and I must wait for Pa's arrival.'"
“Baisu is compassionate and benevolent; he is concerned for the ten directions. Knowing that my country is desolate, he will surely come.
The messenger received his orders and went to where Baisu was, prostrating himself and saying:

“The Great King sends his most earnest and boundless respects. He acknowledges his own transgressions as being grave and heavy, having failed to heed your holy intentions, thereby causing the land to fall into ruin and the people to suffer in poverty. Weeping for you, he can neither eat nor drink.”
"I pray you will deign to show me compassion and come to see me once more!
Out of pity for the people, the Paṇḍita returned with the messenger.
On the way, he saw a dead monkey; he therefore skinned it so that he might speak with a living voice.
When the people of the kingdom heard that the Seer (Bodhisattva) had arrived, they all went beyond the borders to welcome him.
Upon reaching the outskirts of the city, the Seer stayed at his former monastery.
The King came out to meet him; after performing his salutations and inquiries, he sat down to one side and, with palms joined, apologized to the Seer, saying:
"Kong Wan was incompetent and cruelly oppressed the myriad people; I beg to repent and exert myself from now on, hoping you will grant me clemency!
The Parrot said, "Very well."
The four ministers whispered behind his back, and the Parantapa said:
"You have done no wrong; why do you not speak openly?
The four ministers replied in anger:
"Anyone who has become a śramaṇa and desires heavenly merit, whom all people praise as virtuous, ought not to kill a monkey to take its skin.
The Paṇḍita said, "You yourselves are deluded; you simply fail to distinguish between the true and the false."
Whether right or wrong, good or evil, Heaven knows them all;
suffering and joy have their roots and cannot be overcome by force.
When one commits evil, the retribution follows; though much time may pass, it is not dissolved.
When one performs good, blessings follow; in the end, there is no ruin.
Fortune and calamity reside within oneself, yet the foolish claim they are distant.
Because I flayed my skin to kill this monkey, this difficulty seems plausible; yet, [the principle remains that] fortune and calamity reside within oneself, though the foolish deem them remote.
"You all remain silent while committing evil without ceasing; do you teach one another that fate is determined by Heaven, and that doing good brings no benefit while doing evil incurs no calamity?
The retribution of misfortune and fortune occurs naturally like an echo; the echo follows the sound—it does not fall from the sky."
"You all have committed evil; do you not recognize this yourselves?
Though you wish to slander me, I naturally will not listen.
This is not an admonition to me, but rather it strikes you yourselves."
When you alone say, "When a person dies, they perish and are not reborn," is this the word of a sage?
Or does it issue from your own mind?
It is because you yourself wish to do evil that you conversely claim that performing good brings no merit and committing evil incurs no calamity.
"Now, as for the luminous phenomena of Heaven—the sun, moon, and stars arrayed above—who created them?
The four ministers remained silent.
The Parable-Speaker (Pai) spoke again:
"Between heaven and earth, all things arise solely from sin and merit.

When a person performs good or evil, it is like a shadow following a form. Though the dead cast off their bodies, their deeds do not perish; it is like planting grain: the seed decays below, yet the roots, stems, leaves, and fruit emerge above."
The continuity of formative action (*saṃskāra*) is like a lamp or a candle: as one flame is lit after another, the wick may be consumed, yet the fire continues without ceasing.
Thus, though actions involve both demerit and merit, they persist like characters written by someone at night that remain even after the light has gone out.
The soul-spirit follows along, undergoing successive births without interruption.
Your intentions, you consider yourselves noble;
yet if one were to kill their own parent, could they truly be without sin?
The four ministers replied, "One does not pluck the leaves from that which provides shade for its branches; how much less could one kill a kinsman and remain without guilt? Pa said:
"However, your challenge of me seems quite plausible.
I take even dead skin and still question it; as for what you gentlemen do, how should the law regard it?
You alone say: 'When a person dies, they perish and are not born again.'"
One person said, "Suffering and happiness depend on heaven";
another said, "Doing good brings no merit, and committing evil incurs no calamity";
yet another relied on his own knowledge of astrology.
Outwardly manifesting yang is goodness; inwardly harboring yin is villainy.
It is like counterfeit gold, which is pure copper within;
its appearance is adorned with beautiful words, yet its mind and actions are slanderous and treacherous.
It is like a wolf among sheep that its master fails to perceive.

So too are the wicked people of the world who claim to be followers of the Way; with disheveled hair lying upon the ground, they preach the scriptures and precepts while practicing nothing but flattery and deception, greedily seeking profit and gain.
The ignorant believe and submit like rain settling dust.
The various demons become weary of one another like overflowing waters that, failing to enter the sea at the proper time, cause much injury and ruin.
Only the Sage is able to deliver the world, transforming evil and bestowing goodness, so that none fail to receive his protection.
If there were no blessings for good and no calamities for evil, why would the ancient sages have composed the scriptures and bestowed the sharp sword upon kings?
Now, actions have their retributions; this law is natural: the good receive blessings, and the evil receive calamity.
That which Heaven hastens toward brings misfortune without long delay; though hidden virtues may remain concealed, they will not fail to provide protection in the future.

Therefore, the state establishes a king, and the king’s governance accords with Heaven: he employs the worthy and utilizes the capable, rewards the good and punishes the wicked; each acts according to their deeds, like an echo responding to a sound.
When a person dies and the spirit departs, it follows one's conduct to be reborn, just as a chariot wheel turns without ever leaving the ground.
Truly, the retribution of sin and merit cannot be denied.
When a person acts with utmost sincerity, the spirits and deities assist them.

Though one may not immediately perceive evil, one will inevitably suffer its retribution in the end; therefore, one should be cautious and vigilant, distancing oneself from evil and maintaining a sense of shame.
If all were to do good, they would naturally receive a uniform endowment of vital energy (*qi*).

Yet, those who are not virtuous are often unequal: some live long while others die young; some suffer many ailments while others remain largely healthy; some are ugly while others are handsome; some are poor while others are wealthy and noble; and there is an uneven distribution of the wise and the foolish. There are even those who are blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired, as well as those with crippled limbs, lameness, or physical deformities—all of which result from the evil deeds committed in previous lives.
That one receives the hundred blessings—which are what people delight in—is due to having practiced goodness in previous lives.

That there are the sun, moon, and stars; that there are devas, humans, emperors, kings, and the noble and wealthy, is clear evidence of this. These result from the accumulation of merit and loyal governance.
"How can you say it does not exist?
You should reflect upon this thoroughly; do not say otherwise.
When the Paṇḍita spoke these words, the king, his ministers, and the common people were all moved to understanding and joy.
The Parantapa spoke again:
"In ancient times there was a king named Shva-jita.
In his pond grew sweet fish, delicious and with few bones."
The king appointed one person to oversee them, ordering that eight fish be offered daily.
That overseer also secretly ate eight fish each day.
When the king noticed the fish were diminishing, he established eight overseers and ordered them to guard them together.
Furthermore, if eight supervisors each day steal eight fish, and those who guard them are many, the fish will be exhausted.
Now Your Majesty is like this: those you employ are not few, yet the disorder increases all the more.
It is like a person who plucks raw fruit; having destroyed its seed, it will have no flavor when eaten.
If a king desires to govern but does not employ worthy men, he will lose his people and subsequently lack merit.
If the governance of a state is not upright, it will cause the world to harbor hearts of contention and plunder.
It is like a person managing their property who does not apply diligent effort; then their wealth will diminish day by day.
If a state possesses those who are brave and martial and trained in battle formations, yet fails to satisfy their aspirations, it will weaken the state.

If one acts as a ruler without reverence for the Way and its Virtue, and does not serve those of lofty brilliance, then while alive, the worthy will not come to him; and after death, his spirit will not ascend to Heaven.
To plunder and kill the innocent, causing the world to harbor resentment and lodge complaints, brings down calamities from Heaven and causes one to lose their good reputation.

To govern a state by law, conduct administration with loyalty, respect elders and love the young, practice filial piety and obedience, and uphold what is virtuous, will result in peace and security in the present life and rebirth in heaven after death.
It is like the path taken by a lead ox: if its course is straight and correct, all other oxen will follow it.
When a noble leader possesses the Way and guides his subordinates with rectitude, those far and near will submit and be transformed, thereby bringing about great peace.

As a ruler, you ought to be enlightened, investigating the past and understanding the present; you must know the proper timing for action and stillness, and ensure that firmness and flexibility accord with principle; you should bestow kindness upon those below to benefit the people, distributing your favors with impartiality.
"In this way, you will be noble and honored life after life, and later attain the Way of Nirvana.
All those seated there rejoiced and praised him boundlessly.
The King immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself, and said:
"What the Parṣva has just said is like a swift wind blowing away clouds and rain.
We pray that you will finally maintain your compassionate regard and bestow your transformative influence as before.
Thereupon, the Parṣva rose and proceeded, following the King into the palace.
The four ministers were foolish and were thus dismissed from office.

Prasenajit once again governed the kingdom; his benevolence flowed forth in abundance, winds and rains came at their proper seasons, the five grains ripened in profusion, and the people rejoiced. People gathered from the four quarters, high and low lived in harmony and joy, and the land eventually attained great peace.
The Buddha said,
"The one who was Paṭa at that time is my current self.
The practitioner who was my sister’s son is Ānanda."
The King Lambada of that time was none other than the present Vipaśyin;
the Queen of that time was Śirīṣā;
and the dog Bhṛṅgī was none other than Chandaka.
The four great ministers at that time were these four men who killed Hao-shou;
the frog who spoke at that time was this Udayin, who has now attained arhatship.

As a bodhisattva, I have practiced goodness life after life, diligently accumulating merit for incalculable eons; for the sake of the myriad people, I have now personally attained Buddhahood, and all my aspirations have been fulfilled.
"All those who encounter me and hear this Dharma of the sutra should each apply themselves with diligence; perform good deeds and do not be indolent.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, three hundred million people attained the fruit of entering the Path, all received the five precepts, and joyfully practiced them.
An Excerpt from the *Fo shuo pai jing* (The Sutra on Pai Spoken by the Buddha)
